title: "Hypothesis Test: Introduction with Bootstrapping"
format: pdf
editor: visual
---

## Situation

Suppose we know the heights of everyone in a population of 10,000 people. We want to evaluate the heights of some sample of 20 people from the population and determine if their heights are different from those in the population. We will conduct a hypothesis test using bootstrapping. As such, we need to do the following:

- Define the problem
- Collect data or run experiment
- Choose a model for testing
- Perform test/model
- Draw conclusions

### Define the Problem

We need to setup the test at first. We care about some population mean of heights $\mu$ and are using the sample mean $\bar{x}$ to test against $\mu_0$, which is the common belief about the population mean. In our case, we say that $\mu_0 = 67.5$.

Next, we can denote the hypotheses. We want to look for a difference, and as such:

- $H_0: \mu = 67.5$
- $H_a: \mu \neq 67.5$

Lastly, we define a discernibility level of 0.05.

## Collect Data

We have the data itself from the sample, which is seen below:

```{r}
samp <- c(59, 67, 73, 61, 60, 62, 62, 65, 62, 58, 70, 61, 63, 62, 66, 64, 63, 64, 61, 60)
```

We also know the population itself, whose distribution is related to the null distribution. As such,

```{r}
set.seed(13)
mu <- 67.5
population <- rnorm(10000, mu, 9)
```

(Yes, I am definitely cheating here. The `rnorm` function itself generates observations from some specified normal distribution. Here, I am asking for 10,000 heights from a Normal distribution with mean 67.5 and variance 9.)

**Note:** The `set.seed()` function is useful for replication of randomized results. Put in a random number inside the function and as long as you run that function (with its number) in the same run as your randomized code, you will get the same results. Try it!

## Choose and Perform the Model

We will use a bootstrap here to ultimately get a $p$-value. A bootstrap is possible to acquire the $p$-value here since we know the population/null distribution. Otherwise, we would need to perform a randomization test or a classic technique. To perform the test, we will need to pull $B$ bootstrap samples from the population itself of size 20. We want to see: is our sample of 20 much different from the many samples of 20 from the population?

To do so in R, we use a for-loop. A for-loop is designed to repeat the same process over and over again. We usually store results from each iteration into some data structure, which is why you see `res[i]` referenced inside the for-loop -- this is how we store the mean of some ith sample of heights.

We want to retrieve many bootstrap samples, so we set $B = 1000$. We can then run the bootstrapping below:

```{r}
# Number of bootstrap samples
B <- 1000

# Stores sample means of heights
res <- rep(-1, B)

# For loop that goes from 1 to B; samples 20 from population, then finds sample mean of heights
for (i in 1:B){
  pop_samp <- sample(population, 20)
  res[i] <- mean(pop_samp)
}
```

To then find our $p$-value, we then need to what proportion of sample means from the bootstrap samples are more extreme than the sample mean of interest (i.e. the test statistic). Since we have a two-sided test, we look at differences on both sides of the population mean. This means:

- If $\bar{x}_b \leq \mu_0 - d$, then it is more extreme
- If $\bar{x}_b \geq \mu_0 + d$, then it is more extreme

$d$ is denoted as the absolute difference between $\mu_0$ and $\bar{x}$. Visually, we want to find the probability of being either to the left of the red line or to the right of the blue line:

```{r}
xbar <- mean(samp)
diff <- abs(xbar - mu)

hist(res, main = "Sampling Distribution of Heights", xlab = "Height")
abline(v = mu - diff, col = "red")
abline(v = mu + diff, col = "blue")
```

We just take the proportion of sample means more extreme than our sample mean, which is:

```{r}
pval <- mean(res <= mu - diff | res >= mu + diff)
```

## Draw Conclusions

```{r}
pval
```

Our p-value is equal to 0.028, which is less than our discernibility level of 0.05. As such, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is a discernible difference in the mean heights of this group versus the heights in the population.
